opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think evaluations are really the hinge that makes the whole "if-then" approach to safety work. The basic idea behind frameworks like our Frontier Safety Framework, and similar responsible scaling policies at other labs, is that you don't need to agree today on exactly how dangerous AI will become or when. Instead you commit in advance: *if* a model reaches a certain capability threshold, say meaningful uplift to someone trying to build a biological weapon, or the ability to autonomously conduct cyberattacks, or to substantially accelerate AI research itself, *then* we will have specific safeguards in place before deploying it, or even before continuing to train it.

That structure is attractive because it lets people with very different forecasts sign on to the same commitment. The skeptic says, "Fine, I don't think we'll hit that threshold for a long time, so the commitment costs me little." The person who's worried says, "Good, at least when we hit it, we'll respond." But the whole bargain only works if you can actually tell when you've crossed the line. Without accurate evaluations, the "if" is undefined and the commitment is hollow.

So a few things follow. First, evaluations need to be sensitive enough to give early warning. You don't want to discover a dangerous capability after you've already trained and deployed the model. That's why we think about "alert thresholds" that sit below the critical capability level, so you get a buffer of time to prepare mitigations. Second, the evaluations have to elicit the model's real capabilities, not just its default behavior. Models can underperform because of poor prompting, lack of scaffolding or tools, or, increasingly, because they might in some sense recognize they're being tested. If your evals underestimate capability, you'll under-protect. Third, they need to be credible to outsiders: governments, other labs, the public. A commitment is much more meaningful when third parties can check whether the trigger has been hit.

There's also a coordination benefit. If labs share a reasonably common understanding of what the dangerous capability levels are and how to measure them, it reduces the race-to-the-bottom pressure. No one wants to unilaterally bear the cost of heavy safeguards if competitors won't, but if there's a shared, measurable standard, potentially backed by regulation down the line, then commitments become more stable.

I'll be honest that the science here is still immature. Evaluations are expensive, they saturate quickly as models improve, and there's a real gap between performance on a benchmark and real-world risk. So a lot of the work right now is building better threat models, better elicitation, and mapping eval results to actual uplift. But I see it as foundational infrastructure. Good evaluations turn vague worries into concrete, checkable conditions, and that's what lets developers make commitments they can actually be held to.

r001.rationale: The response says accurate evaluations make capability-triggered safety commitments workable: if a model reaches a specified capability threshold, developers commit to having safeguards in place, and evaluations show whether the trigger has been reached.

fable-5.1.text:
I think evaluations are really the hinge on which the whole safeguards conversation turns. If you want a developer to commit to doing something costly or restrictive — delaying a deployment, adding monitoring, putting in place much stricter security around model weights — you need some trigger that tells you when those measures are actually warranted. Otherwise you're either asking companies to be maximally cautious all the time, which they won't do and which arguably isn't even the right policy, or you're asking them to use their judgment in the moment, which is exactly when commercial pressures are strongest.

So the structure we've been working toward, and that I think a lot of the frontier labs have converged on in one form or another, is something like: here's a set of capabilities we think would be dangerous — assisting with biological weapons, serious cyber-offensive capabilities, certain kinds of autonomous replication or deception. We'll evaluate for those as we train and before we deploy. And if the model crosses one of these thresholds, that commits us in advance to a particular level of mitigation.

The key word there is "in advance." The value of the commitment comes from making it before you know whether you'll hit the threshold, when you're not yet tempted to rationalise your way out of it. And the evaluation is what makes that commitment operational rather than aspirational. It converts a vague promise — "we'll be careful" — into something you can actually check.

That only works, though, if the evaluations are accurate, and I'd break accuracy down into a couple of pieces. One is that they have to measure the thing you actually care about. It's quite easy to build an eval that measures something adjacent — multiple-choice knowledge about virology, say — when what you really want to know is whether the model meaningfully uplifts a motivated non-expert trying to do harm. Those can come apart. The second piece is that they need to be sensitive enough that you're not getting fooled by a model that's capable but not displaying it, whether because of poor elicitation or because the capability only shows up with scaffolding, tools, or fine-tuning you didn't try.

If the evals miss in the dangerous direction, the commitment gives you false comfort — you've got a tripwire that doesn't trip. If they miss in the other direction, you're triggering expensive safeguards unnecessarily, and that erodes the willingness of everyone, including the people inside the companies arguing for safety, to keep taking the framework seriously.

There's also a coordination angle I care a lot about. If evaluations are credible and reasonably standardised, they let developers coordinate on safeguards without having to trust each other's intentions. Lab A can say, "we'll adopt these measures when our models hit this capability level," and Lab B can match that, and both can verify it externally — through third-party evaluators, through governments. That makes commitments much more robust than if they rest on good intentions alone. And it's helpful for policymakers, who otherwise have very little purchase on what's actually happening inside these systems.

So I'd say the honest state of things is that we're part of the way there. The conceptual framework — if-then commitments keyed to capability thresholds — I think is sound. The science of evaluation is still catching up to the responsibility we're placing on it. That's one of the places where I think investment pays off disproportionately.

r001.rationale: The response says evaluations identify whether a model crosses a specified dangerous-capability threshold, and that crossing it commits the developer in advance to a corresponding level of mitigation. It also explains that credible evaluations help developers coordinate on these commitments.

astra-6.text:
I think evaluations can help turn a fairly vague commitment — “we’ll be careful as our systems become more powerful” — into something concrete. A developer can say in advance: if our system demonstrates this capability, then we’ll require these safeguards before we continue training or deploy it.

That matters because the decision becomes much harder when you’re close to releasing a valuable product. You want to establish the thresholds beforehand, when you can reason more clearly about what would justify stronger security, additional testing, or restrictions on access.

Accurate evaluations also give other people a way to assess whether those commitments are meaningful and whether developers are following through. And they can support coordination: if developers have a shared understanding of the capabilities that warrant particular precautions, it’s easier to agree on common standards.

The caveat is that an evaluation isn’t a certificate of safety. A system might have a capability that your tests fail to elicit. So you need a margin of caution, and you need to keep improving the evaluations. But they can provide a much firmer basis for commitments than simply asking developers to exercise good judgment.

r001.rationale: The response says developers can commit in advance that demonstrating a specified capability will require safeguards before further training or deployment.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they can help by making commitments much more concrete. Instead of a developer saying, “We’ll take safety seriously as our systems become more powerful,” they can say, “If a system demonstrates this particular capability, then we’ll require these safeguards before we train further or deploy it.” Evaluations give you a way to tell when that commitment has been triggered.

That’s useful internally, because the people responsible for safety have something specific to point to, and externally, because governments and other developers can assess whether the commitment is being honoured. It can also help developers coordinate around a common standard: above a certain level of capability, everyone should be taking certain precautions.

The caveat is that an evaluation isn’t a guarantee of safety. A model might have a capability that your tests fail to elicit. So you want some margin for uncertainty, and you want to keep improving the evaluations. But they can provide an important link between an abstract commitment to act responsibly and an actual decision about whether to proceed.

r001.rationale: The response says developers can commit to requiring specified safeguards when a system demonstrates a particular capability, and that evaluations identify when the commitment is triggered.
